title: Reading the position and making a plan

bank.prompt: A rook and seven pawns each, so the mismatch is the minor pieces. Tap the black piece that can move to exactly 2 squares.
bank.reason: The bishop on e7 has 2 squares and its own pawns on d6 and f6 hold both diagonals. The knight on d2 has 5. Play where your half of the pair is the better half.

bank.prompt: A rook and seven pawns each, so the mismatch is the minor pieces. Tap the black piece that can move to exactly 2 squares.
bank.reason: The bishop on e7 has 2 squares and its own pawns on d6 and f6 hold both diagonals. The knight on d2 has 5. Play where your half of the pair is the better half.

bank.prompt: The bishop on e7 has 2 squares. Tap every white piece that has more than that.
bank.reason: d2 and e1 all have more room than that bishop. Naming both halves of the pair is what turns a judgement into a plan.

bank.prompt: Material is level and a knight faces a bishop. Which mismatch gives White his plan?
options: White has an extra pawn on the queenside.
Black's rook stands on the better file, so there is nothing for White here.
The bishop on e7 has 2 squares against the knight's 5, so White plays to keep it shut in.
bank.reason: White's queenside pawns are a3, b2, c3 against a7, b7, c7: level, not an extra pawn. The piece count is the mismatch.

bank.prompt: Each side has an extra pawn on one wing. Tap every white pawn on the a, b and c files.
bank.reason: Three against two: a2, b2, c3 against a7 and b7. That is the wing this side plays on.

bank.prompt: Each side has an extra pawn on one wing. Tap every black pawn on the f, g and h files.
bank.reason: Three against two: f7, g7, h7 against f2 and g2. That is the wing this side plays on.

bank.prompt: A rook and five pawns each, and a knight against a bishop. Which pair tells each side where to play?
options: White has three pawns to two on the queenside and Black three to two on the kingside, so each plays where he has the extra pawn.
White's pawns are all on the queenside and Black's all on the kingside.
Neither side has more pawns than the other on either wing.
bank.reason: Queenside it is a2, b2, c3 against a7 and b7; kingside f7, g7, h7 against f2 and g2. Both sides have a majority, on opposite wings.

bank.prompt: Start with the count that decides which wing is yours. Tap every white man standing on the f, g or h file.
bank.reason: 6 white men against Black's 5 on those three files. The king counts: he is a defender on that side of the board.

bank.prompt: A pawn chain points wherever its front pawn looks. Tap the white pawn that attacks two squares on the sixth rank.
bank.reason: The pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6. No other white pawn reaches the sixth rank, so that is the direction the chain points.

bank.prompt: Both counts are done. Which side of the board is White's, and what says so?
options: The queenside, because White has more pawns there.
The kingside: 6 white men on the f, g and h files against 4, and the pawn on e5 points that way.
Neither wing: the pawn structure is the same on both sides of the board.
bank.reason: Queenside it is 2 men each, so nobody has more. And the structures differ: White stands on e5 and f4, Black on d5 and e6.

bank.prompt: Now his half of the sum. Tap every black man standing on the f, g or h file.
bank.reason: 4 against White's 6. One extra man on the wing you are working on is the whole of this advantage.

bank.prompt: Other wing, same question. Tap every white man standing on the a, b or c file.
bank.reason: 5 white men against 2. Both rooks are already there, which is what makes this wing the one to open.

bank.prompt: Which side of the board is White's here, and why?
options: The kingside, because that is where the black king lives.
Neither wing: material is dead level, so there is nothing to aim at.
The queenside: 5 white men on the a, b and c files against 2, and three pawns against two.
bank.reason: On the kingside White has 4 men against 5, so that is his opponent's wing, king or no king. Level material is not a level board.

bank.prompt: Pawns only this time. Tap every white pawn on the a, b or c file.
bank.reason: a2, b3, c4 against a7 and b7. Three against two on the wing where your rooks already stand is the clearest instruction you will get.

bank.prompt: Material is level. What should decide which wing White works on?
options: The man count: 5 white men to 2 on the a, b and c files, against 4 to 4 on f, g and h.
Whichever wing the enemy king is nearest, always.
Nothing should: with level material either wing is as good as the other.
bank.reason: The two counts disagree with each other, and that disagreement is the answer. 5 against 2 one side, 4 against 4 the other.

bank.prompt: Black has 29 legal moves. One white move cuts him to 2. Tap the square the rook goes to.
bank.reason: Rd8+ is White's only check, so Black may only answer it: 2 legal replies instead of 29. The next best white move still leaves him 26.

bank.prompt: Black has 27 legal moves. One white move cuts him to 2. Tap the square the rook goes to.
bank.reason: Rd8+ is White's only check, so Black may only answer it: 2 legal replies instead of 27. The next best white move still leaves him 24.

bank.prompt: Rd8+ cuts Black from 23 answers to 2. Why is it still a bad move?
options: Because a check is never worth playing while the opponent still has a bishop.
One of those answers takes the rook on d8, and no white man defends it.
Because the black king simply walks out of it to h8.
bank.reason: Nothing white covers d8, so the check costs a whole rook. And h8 is not an escape: the king would still be on the checking rook's rank.

bank.prompt: Forcing and good are not the same word. What does counting his replies actually tell you?
options: That the move with the fewest replies is always the best move.
Nothing useful, because the number of replies has no bearing on a plan.
Only how much choice he has left: Rd8+ leaves him 2 answers out of 23, and you still have to count what it costs.
bank.reason: A forcing move buys you his attention, not material. Rd8+ is forcing and loses a rook; the count and the cost are two separate sums.

bank.prompt: Two black men hit your rook and nothing defends it. Answer him with the move that asks a bigger question.
bank.reason: Rxb5 steps out of the fork and takes a bishop that no black man defends. One move, both jobs, and now he is the one answering.

bank.prompt: Work out who is asking the questions. Tap every black man that attacks the white rook on d5.
bank.reason: e6 and f6, and no white man defends d5. Having the move is not the same as having the initiative.

bank.prompt: It is White to move. Who holds the initiative, and what follows from it?
options: Black does: e6 and f6 both hit the rook and nothing defends it, so White must move it — and should take something on the way.
White does, because it is White's turn to move.
Nobody: the rook on d5 is defended, so there is nothing to answer.
bank.reason: No white man defends d5. The rook has to move, and the square to move it to is the one with a black bishop on it.

bank.prompt: Black has no check and no capture anywhere, and he still has a plan. Tap the square his b-pawn is heading for.
bank.reason: b5 attacks the pawn on c4, and the pawn on a6 is already there to back it up. Name the square and his whole idea becomes something you can take away.

bank.prompt: His pawn is coming to b5 and one white pawn covers that square. Tap the square a white pawn goes to so that two of them do.
bank.reason: a4 is the only pawn move in the position that makes it two. It attacks nothing and threatens nothing; it just removes his idea.

bank.prompt: Black has no check and no capture. What is he preparing on the queenside?
options: Nothing: a man with no check and no capture has no plan.
b5, which the pawn on a6 supports and which hits the pawn on c4.
Nxe4, winning a pawn.
bank.reason: b5 is legal now and a6 is already behind it. Nxe4 is not even legal here: e4 is an empty square, because White's pawn stands on e3.

bank.prompt: His break is coming to b5. Leaving the b-pawn itself aside, tap every black man that already covers that square.
bank.reason: a6. A break with a man behind it is a plan; a break with nothing behind it is a pawn you can just take.

bank.prompt: White answers his plan with the quiet move a4, taking the break square away. Is the pawn safe there?
reasons: Yes. No black man touches a4 at all.
No. The pawn on a6 takes it.
No. The knight reaches c5 and hits it.
bank.reason: Nothing of Black's attacks a4: the pawn on a6 captures forwards on to b5, and c5 is covered by White's own pawn on d4, so the knight cannot go there either.

reasons: No. The pawn on a6 takes it.
Yes. No black man touches a4 at all.
No. The knight reaches c5 and hits it.
bank.reason: Nothing of Black's attacks a4: the pawn on a6 captures forwards on to b5, and c5 is covered by White's own pawn on d4, so the knight cannot go there either.

bank.prompt: His checks and captures come back empty. Which question should you ask instead?
options: Whether he has a check next move, asked again more carefully.
Which of his pieces is worth the most.
What square do his next few moves need — here b5, with the pawn on a6 behind it and the pawn on c4 in front.
bank.reason: The scan for checks and captures is about next move and it has already answered. A plan lives three or four moves out, and it always needs a square.

bank.prompt: White wants a piece on d6 and no black pawn can ever attack it again. Tap every black man that still covers d6.
bank.reason: Only the bishop on e7. Not one of the other 10 black men touches d6, and no black pawn will ever be able to: that would need a pawn on c7 or e7, and both have gone past.

bank.prompt: No black pawn will ever reach d6 again, and one black piece still guards it. Tap the piece you want to swap off.
bank.reason: The bishop on e7 is the only man covering d6, so it is the only swap on the board that changes anything about that square.

bank.prompt: Material is dead level and nothing is loose. Which swap turns d6 into something White can use?
options: Bxe7, because that bishop is the only black man covering d6.
Nd5, planting the knight in the middle of the board.
Bh6, to strip the pawn cover off his king.
bank.reason: Nd5 is met by a pawn capture and Bh6 by gxh6 for nothing. Bxe7 is answered by a recapture and is a real swap, and it is the only one that touches d6.

bank.prompt: Make the swap, let him take back, then collect the square you paid for.
bank.reason: Bxe7 Rxe7 Rd6. Nothing black covers d6 once that bishop has gone, and no black pawn will ever be able to, so the rook there is permanent.

bank.prompt: White goes looking for a swap and offers one with Bh6. Is the piece safe there?
reasons: Yes. Black cannot afford to take.
Yes. It is defended twice over.
No. gxh6 is legal and it costs White a piece.
bank.reason: undefended, g7 takes it. Sound comes first and useful comes second: this one is not even sound.

bank.prompt: White goes looking for a swap and offers one with Nd5. Is the piece safe there?
reasons: No. cxd5 or exd5 is legal and it costs White a piece.
Yes. Black cannot afford to take.
Yes. It is defended twice over.
bank.reason: cheaper taker (1 for 3). Sound comes first and useful comes second: this one is not even sound.

bank.prompt: The swap on e7 costs a bishop and gains no material at all. What does it actually buy?
options: A pawn, once the recapture has been made.
The square d6, which no black man will cover once that bishop has gone and no black pawn can ever attack.
Nothing: with material level after it, the swap is a waste of a move.
bank.reason: The bishop on e7 is the only guard of d6. Material stays level through the whole swap; what changes hands is one square that cannot be taken back.
